craft_claim: Deadpan's origin is the expressionless face of performance (Keaton, vaudeville), and prose cannot reproduce that visual channel: the writer must transfer it into register-stasis and withheld reaction, with an acknowledged loss of the performer's physical timing.

supporting_evidence.location: entry 'deadpan' (quoting a 1928 *New York Times* slang item)
supporting_evidence.note: The 1928 record defines the term as 'playing a role with expressionless face,' citing Buster Keaton — establishing the face, not the sentence, as the original instrument. Tier 5 (as quoted by a reference work); short PD fragment. Recognition only.

supporting_evidence.location: biographical/critical discussion of Keaton's screen persona
supporting_evidence.note: Secondary documentation of the 'great stone face' as a deliberate comic system: the body reacts, the face does not. Tier 3 secondary source; supports the visual-channel claim.

A shared boundary case showing how a controlled, non-reactive narrating voice operates in prose — the structural analogue of the unresponsive face. Cross-link to shared registry; used as a prose-mechanism analogue, not as a deadpan exemplar.

counterevidence.location: discussion of staging and theatrical convention
counterevidence.note: Esslin's account of absurdist theatre implies stage delivery carries meaning through staging conventions that prose simply does not have — the transfer is a rebuild, not a transcription. Reinforces the limit: prose must invent substitutes rather than borrow the stage's.

scope: Any adaptation of deadpan from visual or performed media into prose (film novelization, stage-to-page, screenplay prose drafts). In native prose the claim is analogical: prose *builds* its own flat surface rather than inheriting one.
exceptions: Illustrated or multimodal text (comics, captioned image) retains a visual channel and can carry the face directly; the transfer limit does not apply there.
